Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

there was a map beside the ticket machines, although the small print was hard to read while people were standing in front of it. i asked a staff member where the north entrance was. she pointed toward a corridor and said, “keep going past the coffee shop, then turn left.” that was clearer than the signs, but i still checked the wall numbers as i walked. i arrived a few minutes before my sister. i felt a little foolish for getting turned around, though the station did have several signs that seemed to give different kinds of directions in the same place. i would probably leave extra time next time, even if i already knew the station better.", "output": "Last Thursday, I got to the bus station early because I was going to meet my sister at the north entrance, and I hadn’t been there in a long time. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "on saturday, october 12, i went to mara's shed behind her house in bellwether, because she had asked if i wanted to help build a kite for the small autumn flying day at the school field. i got there at about 3:10. the rain had stopped, but the ground by the gate was still dark and soft. mara was there with her neighbor eli, and a kettle was already on a camping stove near the open shed door. she said, “we can do the frame first, and if the wind holds off we’ll cover it before you leave.” i had built paper kites as a child, but nothing with a proper sail, so i was not sure what to expect.

inside, the shed smelled like cedar shavings and the orange hand soap mara uses at her workbench. two bicycles were hanging from hooks, and a folded card table had been set up under the long window. on it were bamboo spars, cotton line, a roll of red ripstop nylon, a small tin of brass clips, and a ruler with a chipped corner. mara explained that the kite was meant to be a diamond shape, about thirty inches high, and not a stunt kite. eli had brought a paper pattern from a book, though one corner of it had gone soft from being kept in his coat pocket. we put a mug on each side to hold the paper flat.

mara started by checking the bamboo. she rolled each piece against the table and set aside one that bent more than the others. “it might still work for a smaller kite,” she said, “but we don’t need to make this one fight us.” the main spar was thirty inches long, and the cross spar measured twenty-four. she showed me how to find the middle of each one with the ruler, then marked the points in pencil instead of cutting at once. i held the cross spar while eli wrapped cotton line around the crossing. the first knot slipped, and he laughed that his fingers were still cold from carrying the pieces over.

1. The frame and the bridle
mara tied the spars together at the center and added a short wrap of masking tape so the joint would not shift while we worked. she made me check that the cross spar sat level, and then we bent its ends gently down toward the table. a length of cotton line went from one tip to the other, making the kite’s curved edge. i pulled it too tight on the first try, so the bamboo bowed sharply instead of in a gradual curve. mara loosened it and said, “just enough tension to give the sail a little shape.” we tied a small loop at the top and another at the bottom, then attached a bridle line between them. eli measured the distance with his thumb and said it was close to five inches, which was the measurement in the pattern.

the paper pattern showed a narrow seam allowance, but mara said we should leave a little extra nylon at the edges because the fabric frayed when cut. we laid the red cloth on the table, with its dull side facing up, and placed the frame over it. a paperweight held down one corner while i traced the outline in white pencil. the shed light made the pencil difficult to see near the red cloth, so mara moved the lamp closer. when i cut around the marks, i left about an inch along each side. she checked the shape before we folded the edges over the line and fixed them with small pieces of masking tape. the bottom point came out slightly uneven, although it looked fine when the frame was placed on top again.

we did not have a sewing machine in the shed, so mara stitched the folded edges by hand with red thread. eli fed the thread through a needle and made a knot at the end; it took him two attempts because the thread kept slipping away from the needle. i held the cloth still while mara made small stitches, stopping to turn the fabric at each corner. she said the stitching did not need to look perfect, but it should keep the edge from opening in the air. at the top, she added a tiny square of spare nylon under the loop as reinforcement. she asked me to press it flat with my thumb while she made three extra stitches across it. after that, the sail sat neatly over the frame, with the red fabric pulled smooth but not drum-tight.

for the tail, we cut six strips of blue cloth, each about twelve inches long, and tied them to a longer piece of cotton tape. i tied two of them too close together, and mara moved one so the strips would hang separately. she said the tail was mostly there to steady the kite, not to decorate it, though she liked the blue against the red. eli made a small paper bow from a leftover scrap and asked if we could tie it near the end. mara said, “one bow is fine, but we’ll see how it flies before adding more.” we attached the tail to the lower loop and checked that the bridle did not twist around the spar. a spool of white flying line sat on the windowsill, with a cardboard label that said three hundred feet.

by then, the kettle had boiled dry enough that mara poured fresh water into it and made tea. we stood near the open door while it steeped, watching a strip of cloud move past the church roof. eli said the wind felt steadier than it had at lunch, but he was not certain it would last. mara handed me a mug and asked whether i wanted to try the first launch or have her do it. i said she should launch it and i would hold the line, since i had never handled a kite that size. she nodded, then checked the knots once more and tucked the scissors into a drawer so nobody would step on them.

we walked to the school field with the kite under mara’s arm and the line spool in my coat pocket. the grass was wet enough to darken the knees of my trousers when i knelt to untangle the line. mara held the frame upright while eli stood several yards away with the tail. on her count, he let go and i gave the line a little slack, but the kite dipped to the left and settled on the grass. mara thought the bridle might be pulling unevenly. we checked it and found the line had slipped against one of the small brass clips. she moved the clip a little, and i held the two bridle sides level while she tightened it. the second try went higher, though it came down again when the wind eased. nobody treated that as a failure; we gathered the line slowly and looked over the stitching before packing up.

back at the shed, mara wrote the date on the inside of the cardboard pattern and put the unused blue strips in a tin. she said we could try again on the school field if the weather was clearer, and eli offered to bring a longer length of tail tape next time. i carried the kite to the car with the bamboo frame still joined, careful not to catch the red cloth on the door. i left with the tea taste still in my mouth and a small spot of white pencil on my sleeve. the visit took longer than i expected, but i liked seeing how a kite depended on several quiet adjustments rather than one clever trick.", "output": "On Saturday, October 12, I went to Mara’s shed behind her house in Bellwether. She had asked if I wanted to help build a kite for the small autumn flying day at the school field. I arrived at about 3:10. The rain had stopped, but the ground by the gate was still dark and soft. Mara was there with her neighbor Eli, and a kettle was already on a camping stove near the open shed door. She said, “We can do the frame first, and if the wind holds off we’ll cover it before you leave.” I had built paper kites as a child, but nothing with a proper sail, so I wasn’t sure what to expect.

Inside, the shed smelled of cedar shavings and the orange hand soap Mara uses at her workbench. Two bicycles hung from hooks, and a folded card table stood under the long window. On it were bamboo spars, cotton line, a roll of red ripstop nylon, a small tin of brass clips, and a ruler with a chipped corner. Mara explained that the kite was meant to be diamond-shaped, about thirty inches high, and not a stunt kite. Eli had brought a paper pattern from a book, though one corner had gone soft from being kept in his coat pocket. We put a mug on each side to hold the paper flat.

Mara started by checking the bamboo. She rolled each piece against the table and set aside one that bent more than the others. “It might still work for a smaller kite,” she said, “but we don’t need to make this one fight us.” The main spar was thirty inches long, and the cross spar measured twenty-four. She showed me how to find the middle of each with the ruler, then marked the points in pencil instead of cutting right away. I held the cross spar while Eli wrapped cotton line around the crossing. The first knot slipped, and he laughed, saying his fingers were still cold from carrying the pieces over.

1. The frame and the bridle

Mara tied the spars together at the center and added a short wrap of masking tape so the joint wouldn’t shift while we worked. She had me check that the cross spar sat level, then we gently bent its ends down toward the table. A length of cotton line ran from one tip to the other, forming the kite’s curved edge. I pulled it too tight on the first try, so the bamboo bowed sharply instead of forming a gradual curve. Mara loosened it and said, “Just enough tension to give the sail a little shape.” We tied a small loop at the top and another at the bottom, then attached a bridle line between them. Eli measured the distance with his thumb and said it was close to five inches, the measurement in the pattern.

The paper pattern showed a narrow seam allowance, but Mara said we should leave a little extra nylon at the edges because the fabric frayed when cut. We laid the red cloth on the table with its dull side facing up and placed the frame over it. A paperweight held down one corner while I traced the outline in white pencil. The shed light made the pencil difficult to see against the red cloth, so Mara moved the lamp closer. When I cut around the marks, I left about an inch along each side. She checked the shape before we folded the edges over the line and secured them with small pieces of masking tape. The bottom point came out slightly uneven, although it looked fine when we placed the frame on top again.

We didn’t have a sewing machine in the shed, so Mara stitched the folded edges by hand with red thread. Eli threaded a needle and made a knot at the end; it took him two attempts because the thread kept slipping away from the needle. I held the cloth still while Mara made small stitches, stopping to turn the fabric at each corner. She said the stitching didn’t need to look perfect, but it should keep the edge from opening in the air. At the top, she added a tiny square of spare nylon beneath the loop for reinforcement. She asked me to press it flat with my thumb while she made three extra stitches across it. After that, the sail sat neatly over the frame, with the red fabric smooth but not drum-tight.

For the tail, we cut six strips of blue cloth, each about twelve inches long, and tied them to a longer piece of cotton tape. I tied two too close together, so Mara moved one to let the strips hang separately. She said the tail was mostly there to steady the kite, not decorate it, though she liked the blue against the red. Eli made a small paper bow from a leftover scrap and asked if we could tie it near the end. Mara said, “One bow is fine, but we’ll see how it flies before adding more.” We attached the tail to the lower loop and checked that the bridle wasn’t twisted around the spar. A spool of white flying line sat on the windowsill, with a cardboard label that said three hundred feet.

By then, the kettle had boiled dry enough that Mara poured fresh water into it and made tea. We stood near the open door while it steeped, watching a strip of cloud move past the church roof. Eli said the wind felt steadier than it had at lunch, but he wasn’t certain it would last. Mara handed me a mug and asked whether I wanted to try the first launch or have her do it. I said she should launch it and I’d hold the line, since I’d never handled a kite that size. She nodded, checked the knots once more, and tucked the scissors into a drawer so nobody would step on them.

We walked to the school field with the kite under Mara’s arm and the line spool in my coat pocket. The grass was wet enough to darken the knees of my trousers when I knelt to untangle the line. Mara held the frame upright while Eli stood several yards away with the tail. On her count, he let go and I gave the line a little slack, but the kite dipped to the left and settled on the grass. Mara thought the bridle might be pulling unevenly. We checked it and found that the line had slipped against one of the small brass clips. She moved the clip a little, and I held the two sides of the bridle level while she tightened it. The second try went higher, though the kite came down again when the wind eased. Nobody treated that as a failure; we gathered the line slowly and checked the stitching before packing up.

Back at the shed, Mara wrote the date on the inside of the cardboard pattern and put the unused blue strips in a tin. She said we could try again on the school field if the weather was clearer, and Eli offered to bring a longer length of tail tape next time. I carried the kite to the car with the bamboo frame still joined, careful not to catch the red cloth on the door. I left with the taste of tea still in my mouth and a small spot of white pencil on my sleeve. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "last september, Mara and i took the north trail into Alder Basin for three nights, and i brought a gravity camping filter i had bought in spring. i had used it once in the yard, with water from a tap, so that hardly counted as a test. the filter came with a two-liter dirty-water bag, a hollow-fiber cartridge, a short hose, and a backflush syringe. i liked that it could hang from a branch while we made dinner, though i was not sure how much that convenience would matter when we were tired and the ground was uneven.

The first afternoon was dry and warm, and we reached the lower campsite later than planned because we stopped twice to check the paper map at trail junctions. The creek ran below camp, across a strip of slick stones and roots. I filled the bag slowly, trying not to scoop up the brown bits drifting near the bank. Mara held the bag while i attached the hose, and the first drops came through almost immediately. I remember thinking, this is simpler than the instructions made it sound. Then the flow slowed, but not enough that i knew whether anything was wrong.

We hung the bag from a low pine branch, which was only a little higher than my shoulder. The clean hose reached our pot, but it curled against the rim and dripped on the ground until Mara moved the pot closer. While the filter ran, we unpacked food and set up the tent. It took longer than i expected to fill two bottles, maybe because the bag was not very high, but the water looked clear and had no noticeable taste. Mara said, “At least we don’t have to keep walking down there every time we want a drink.” I agreed, though i also noticed how much fiddling it took to get everything hanging without touching the dirt.

On the second morning, i learned that the bag was awkward to fill in the shallow part of the creek. I had to crouch and hold its opening just under the surface, and once i let the edge dip too far and got a little leaf inside. I tipped the water out and started again. The cartridge was easy to connect, but the two ends of the hose looked similar when i was unpacking it, so i checked the small labels before attaching them. I had been sure i would remember which end was which. I did not. That small pause made me less confident in my own preparation than in the filter itself.

1. the things i noticed over the three days
   1. The bag held enough water for both of us to drink and cook, but filling it took more attention than i expected. It was not heavy when empty, which helped, yet its wide opening was hard to manage in moving water.
   2. Hanging the bag worked best when we found a branch at the right height. At our second campsite the branches were either too high or too far from our cooking spot, so we used a sturdy trekking pole between two rocks. It stayed in place, although i watched it more than i needed to.
   3. The filter was quiet and did not need batteries. That mattered more to me than i thought it would. The slow drip gave us time to do other camp jobs, but it also meant we had to plan ahead instead of waiting until a bottle was empty.

That evening, after a windy stretch of trail, the water came through more slowly than it had the day before. I could not tell whether the change was from the creek water, the bag’s height, or something in the cartridge. The instructions said to backflush if the flow slowed, and i used the syringe beside the tent. It was easy to fit, but i worried that i might force the wrong end or spill dirty water on our cooking area. Mara said, “You can do it over there by the rocks.” I did, and afterward the flow seemed faster, although i had not timed it before or after, so that was only my impression.

On our last morning, we were packing in light rain. The bag was damp on the outside, and i wiped it with a bandana before folding it. I kept the cartridge separate from the wet bag in a small plastic pouch, mostly because that was how i had packed it at home. The syringe had a little water in it, and i emptied it before putting it away. I did not know whether i had dried every part properly, and i made a note to read the storage instructions again when i got back. At the trailhead, Mara asked whether i would bring the filter on another trip. I said yes, but i would practice filling and hanging it first, rather than deciding from a clean kitchen counter that i already understood it.

I have used other ways of carrying water, but this was my first trip with a gravity filter, and the experience was less dramatic than i had pictured. Nothing broke, and we did not run out of water. Still, the small practical details stayed in my mind: where the bag could hang, how close the pot had to be, and how quickly i could refill it without dropping something in the creek. I liked having a filter that worked without a pump handle, especially when we were cooking and packing at the same time. I also found myself checking the setup each time, even after it had worked the day before. That caution felt reasonable on the trail, not like a complaint about the equipment. last october i took the ridgeflow squeeze filter on a three-night trip in the north fork area, and i used it for all the water i drank and cooked with. i bought it myself a few weeks before the trip, so this is not a review from somebody who got sent a sample. the filter is a short, firm plastic tube with a cap on each end, a soft squeeze pouch, and a small backflush syringe in the package. the listed weight is 2.1 ounces, and on my kitchen scale the filter and caps came to just under that, without the pouch. i put the pouch and syringe in a separate pocket on the scale, because i wanted to see what i was actually carrying, not because i think the number on the package is wrong.

The first evening, i filled the pouch at a clear creek and had no trouble getting water through the filter. i did have to push harder than i expected, especially when the pouch was full. after a few squeezes, i got into a rhythm: hold the filter over the bottle, keep the pouch close to the opening, and press steadily instead of trying to empty it all at once. my one-liter bottle took about a minute and a half to fill, though that was my timing and not a test with a stopwatch. the water had no noticeable grit or odd taste to me. i drank it plain and used it later for oatmeal and tea.

On the second day, the creek beside camp had a muddy edge where people had stepped into it. i collected water a little upstream, but the pouch still picked up a few bits of leaf and fine sediment. i let the pouch sit for a minute before filtering, which made the larger pieces easier to avoid. the filter did not clog completely, but the squeeze got slower after several refills. i was not sure how much of that was sediment and how much was me squeezing unevenly. at lunch my friend Mara asked, “Is it supposed to take this much effort?” i said i thought it was normal when the water was cloudy, but i couldn't tell her that with certainty.

1. what worked and what didn't
The caps stayed on in my pack, and i didn't find water leaking from the pouch or filter. The pouch opening was wide enough to fill at the creek without using a cup, although holding it open with cold fingers was fiddly. The filter's clean end fit the narrow mouth of my bottle. It also fit the soft flask i brought, but only if i held the flask steady while squeezing. When i set it down on a flat rock, the flask bent and the connection came loose once. That was my mistake as much as a design problem, but it meant i started holding both pieces together every time.

I liked that i could drink directly from the filter, too. On a steep section, i took a drink from the creek through the filter rather than stopping to fill a bottle. The mouthpiece cover is small and easy to misplace, so i kept it attached to the filter with a short cord i already had. The cord is not included. I didn't measure the flow rate or check the filter with laboratory equipment, and i can't say anything about contaminants that aren't visible or noticeable. I followed the package directions about collecting water and cleaning the filter, but this trip doesn't tell me how long it will last.

Cleaning took a little attention at the end of each day. i drew clean water into the syringe and pushed it back through the filter in the direction the instructions show. The syringe worked, but its plunger felt stiff at first, and i had to press it with both thumbs. after i did it a couple times, the movement got easier. i also tapped the filter gently against my palm before putting the caps back on. The package says not to use soap on the filter, so i didn't. The pouch was harder to dry than the filter itself; when i packed up in the morning, a few drops were still inside the seam.

On the last morning, i used the filter at a small pool below a trail crossing. I couldn't see the bottom, and i tried to scoop from the side where the water was moving rather than from the still center. It took more squeezes than at the clear creek on the first night. I had enough patience to finish filling my bottle, but i was glad i wasn't trying to filter a large pot of water quickly. For cooking, i filtered one pouch at a time into a metal cup and poured it into the pot. It worked, though it made the preparation slower than simply using water from a tap at home.

My main complaint is the effort needed to squeeze, especially with cold hands or water that carries sediment. The pouch is useful and lightweight, but it doesn't feel especially robust when full, and i treated it carefully around rocks. I didn't puncture it or notice a seam separating during this trip. The caps and filter body felt more solid than the pouch. I would bring the filter on another short trip because the whole setup packed small and handled my drinking and cooking water, but i would still give myself extra time at cloudy sources and take care not to lose the mouthpiece cover. It's a practical option for the way i camp, with a few small hassles i now know to expect.", "output": "Last October, I took the Ridgeflow squeeze filter on a three-night trip in the North Fork area and used it for all the water I drank and cooked with. i used North Quay bus station on a Thursday just before 10:30, arriving on Route 14 and needing to change to Route 6. My first impression was not especially bad, but it took me a little while to understand how the building was arranged. The board showed route numbers, destinations, and bay numbers, which was useful, but it did not say where the bays were in relation to the hall. A blue sign below it said “Bays 1–8: lower concourse,” and an arrow pointed down a corridor. I followed it and found a staircase and a lift. The lift was working when I was there, and it had room for my suitcase, but there was no sign at the entrance saying whether the lower concourse was also accessible by ramp. I did not need a ramp myself, so I cannot say what the route would be. A smaller sign beside the stairs listed the bay numbers in order, but it was partly hidden behind a temporary notice about a vending machine being out of service.

I spent a few minutes checking that Route 6 really used Bay 5, because the screen at the bottom of the stairs showed only the next four departures. Route 6 was not among them. There was another screen beside the coffee counter, and that one had the full list, but I only noticed it after I had started walking toward Bay 3. A staff member at the counter noticed me looking back and said, “The six is at five today; the board downstairs is just the next departures.” That was helpful, although I would rather have had the same information on both screens. The words “at five today” also made me wonder whether the bay changes often, and I could not find a place nearby that showed any usual bay assignments.

1. Finding the right bay

Once I knew to look for Bay 5, the signs were mostly easy to follow. The numbers above the bays were large, black on yellow, and visible from the center of the concourse. The problem was that the signs were mounted over the platform entrances, not at the point where the corridor split. At the split, there was a small arrow sign saying “1–4 left, 5–8 right.” It was mounted at about eye level, but a group of people waiting near the wall blocked it for a moment. There was no second copy overhead. I went right, as the sign indicated, and could see the number 5 from there, so I did not have to ask anyone again.

The route map near the entrance was useful for understanding which buses went to the neighboring towns, but it was crowded with labels and took me a while to read. It had a “you are here” marker, although the marker was a small red dot over the building outline rather than a label naming the hall. I had to lean closer to tell which side of the station I was on. The map showed the bays, toilets, ticket desks, and the taxi rank outside. It did not show the lift, even though the lift was important for getting to the lower concourse. A separate accessibility sign near the toilets listed an accessible toilet and a help point, but it did not have a map or explain how to reach either one from the entrance.

I also noticed that some information was repeated in different ways. The main board used “Route 6,” while the screen at Bay 5 said “6—Eastfield.” That was not confusing once I knew the destination, but the printed timetable in the clear holder beside the bay called it “Eastfield via Market Road.” I checked the timetable because I was unsure whether it was the same service. The times appeared to match the board, and the paper had a date showing that it was current for that week. A small note said that buses could leave from a different bay during busy periods. I did not see a notice saying which bays were affected, so the note did not give me much help in deciding whether to keep checking.

The staff were approachable when I asked questions. At the information desk, a person in a green vest pointed out the lift and told me where the toilets were, without making me feel that I had asked something obvious. There was a help point beside the ticket desks, but it was close to the wall and partly behind a tall poster. I could see its blue light once I was standing in front of it. I did not use it, so I do not know how quickly someone would answer. The poster advertised a local travel card and covered the lower part of the station map, which made the entrance area feel more cluttered than it needed to be.

For someone with a suitcase, the route from the entrance to the lower concourse was manageable. The floor was level through the hall, and the lift was close to the stairs, rather than around a corner. There were benches near the corridor, though one was occupied by bags while I was there. I saw a parent pushing a stroller use the lift, but I do not know whether every platform can be reached without stairs once you get downstairs. The accessible toilet sign gave a direction but no distance, and the route was not obvious from the place where I first saw it. These gaps may matter more to a passenger who is moving slowly or cannot ask staff for help.

Continuing: holding both pieces together afterward, drinking directly from the filter, scooping from moving water rather than the still center, and noting preparation took longer than tap water at home, so extra time and careful handling were warranted — these all read as reasonable, faithful edits.

Row 029: checking small wording shifts — "was working when I was there" to just "was working" loses a slight temporal hedge, "any usual bay assignments" to "the usual bay assignments" tightens presupposition, and "repeated in different ways" to "presented in different ways" subtly shifts meaning, though these remain minor.
